extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists (students and authors) preparing technical papers and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and copy-editing mathematical and technical prose: organization, grammar, symbol use, punctuation, style, and proof presentation to maximize clarity and avoid distracting the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, coherence, accuracy, and conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: We must strive to be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is especially important; prefer shorter sentences and delete unnecessary words or phrases. Quote: "We must strive to be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise." Read drafts aloud to find verbosity and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do organize; do not distract
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do organize material." "Do not distract the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization is essential though hard to define—recognize good organization when you see it. Spend much of writing time arranging material; weave branches and alternative threads together. Use changes (notation, grammar, repetition) deliberately to jar readers only when desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer more questions than you raise
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing should answer more questions than it raises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentences that create obvious follow-up questions (e.g., 'A solution lies in persuading...' — a solution to what and who persuades?). Be explicit about referents and purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences; minimize semicolons
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut sentences shorter; use periods instead of semicolons except where clauses have a very close relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Out with the semicolons, in with the periods." Semicolons slow pace and convey an old-fashioned tone; use only when clauses are tightly related and a period would be worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject and verb close
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separating subject and verb by many intervening words as such sentences are hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences where the subject and verb are far apart. Example: Rosalie objected to 'Yet many books several hundred years old are in excellent condition' — the subject and verb felt too far apart and raise questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or superfluous words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove words like 'out', gratuitous 'he has heard', and needless noise-phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: replace 'the reason for removing the spaces from the list is that...' with 'We remove the spaces because...'; delete superfluous 'out'; question phrases like 'in the context of' and remove when they add no meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice; use 'we' judiciously or imperatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions; using 'we' to avoid passive voice is common but can add irrelevant tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imperative/indicative or concise constructions instead of 'we' when appropriate: 'Multiply each b.z by this factor' instead of 'Each of the b.z's are then multiplied by this factor.' 'We can now prove...' → 'The following result holds:'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with pronoun references and vague 'it' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sentences beginning with 'It is unlikely...' or other constructions where the pronoun's antecedent is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find alternate constructions that make the subject explicit and remove ambiguous pronoun references so the reader knows what is being referred to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch placement of 'only' (misplacement changes meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misplaced 'only' alters which part of a sentence is being modified and changes meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by inserting 'only' in different positions in 'I hit him in the eye yesterday' — each position produces a different meaning. Prefer the intended placement: e.g., 'Here we calculate the position of only two vertices' instead of 'Here we only calculate the position of two vertices.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague intensifiers like 'really'
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague words such as 'really' are colloquial and can obscure precise technical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific: replace 'saving the computation for the place where it is really needed' with a precise description like 'saving the computation for those vertices where the additional work contributes more to the visual quality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse/repetition of small words (this, they, just, then)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent repetition of common words distracts the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud often helps spot overuse. Rewrite to reduce repeated occurrences of the same small words ('then' repeated many times often stems from code-like phrasing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Anyway, ...', 'pretty straightforward', or 'again iterate through' can sound informal or awkward in technical documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, formal expressions. 'Pretty straightforward' is vague; replace with a concrete description of complexity or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'in the context of' and similar noise-phrases critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether such phrases add meaning; if not, delete them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes repetition of a phrase is useful for clarity (e.g., to signal you're talking about the same thing), so keep when it serves repetition for clarity; otherwise drop as noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas symmetrically for parenthetical notes
rubrics_metrics.description: When using commas to insert a parenthetical, place a comma on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '... this node, b, is thus ...' — ensure both opening and closing commas are present for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise with word choice and avoid commonly conflated pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for frequently-confused words (alternately/alternatively, affect/effect, imply/infer, disinterested/uninterested, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A list of commonly conflated pairs was presented; use the correct term to preserve distinctions that matter to readers. Example explanation: 'Alternately' (one after another) vs 'alternatively' (or else).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation logically (quotation marks, placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place punctuation in a way that makes logical sense rather than blindly following typographic conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Halmos urged placing quotation marks logically. He altered conventions in his books to place punctuation where it made sense to the grammatical structure rather than per typographer's arbitrary rules (example criticizing Turabian/Chicago usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose numeral vs word for clarity (avoid ambiguity of 'one')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '1' when you mean the numeral and 'one' when you mean the pronoun or word sense; avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'What are we to do when x is one?' ambiguous; prefer '1' when speaking of the numeral. 'The number of solutions is either two or three.' vs 'The only solutions are 2 or 3.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Present proofs directly when possible; avoid proof by contradiction for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction should not be used if a direct proof is available; direct proofs usually make for better exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although proofs by contradiction may be convenient for discovery, they can be a circuitous route in presentation. Prefer straightforward direct arguments in written exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grammar (case, 'who' vs 'whom') to clarify logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat grammar as an organizational/logical device; attend to case, tense, and pronoun selection to clarify meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: respect cases ('I don't know him' not 'I don't know he'); prefer nominative 'Who is the President...' rather than 'Whom is the President...'; avoid constructions like 'I hate whomever said that' that violate logical grammatical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid echoing unusual words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat unusual words in unrelated passages because repetition causes unwarranted associations and distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule #9: 'Do not echo unusual words.' Repeating a rare term may cause readers to link unrelated passages or cause typists to omit intervening text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' and first-person carefully; first-person singular discouraged in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of 'we' can ease passive voice but introduces tone; first-person singular can be jarring and is best avoided in formal technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer imperative/indicative or neutral constructions. If tone is desired, 'we' is acceptable but should be used judicially. First-person singular ('I') is often improper in formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about traditional prescriptions (split infinitives, terminal prepositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slavish adherence to prescriptive rules; some traditional rules (avoid splitting infinitives, never end sentences with prepositions) can be counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split infinitives can provide emphasis and acceptable rewrites might sound forced. Ending sentences with prepositions is often harmless and forcing rewrites can be worse; nevertheless consider readability and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exclamation points sparingly and only for real exclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be used only with actual exclamations or interjections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited discourage casual exclamation use. A trick: putting an exclamation point in parentheses (!) indicates surprise while minimizing typographic controversy (anecdotal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep notation and formatting consistent and readable (fractions, hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset mathematics in readable forms (e.g., slashed fractions when appropriate) and be cautious with hyphenation of compound technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward typesetter defaults like n(n+1;(2n+1) and prefer clearer forms. Hyphenation such as 'programming-language notation' may be unnecessary in CS where terms like 'random number generator' are conventional without hyphens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coincident punctuation confusion; follow simple rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincident commas or punctuation marks (comma+period, comma+semicolon) are not signs of bad construction; write only one mark in coincident positions and follow simple precedence rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where two commas coincide, write only one; where comma and period coincide, write the period, etc. Coincident punctuation is not inherently problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward or distracting grammatical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences with nonstandard or distracting grammar ('If I'da knowed...') pull readers away from content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard grammatical forms in technical writing to avoid distracting readers, unless addressing an audience where nonstandard grammar is appropriate for communication.
